phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar [t] plus open [a]; Tahitian t is crisp and unaspirated.
The glottal stop written ʻeta in modern Tahitian — the small catch of breath the older spelling 'Taaroa' silently dropped.
Tapped alveolar [ɾ] followed by the diphthong [oa]; roa means 'long, lasting, far-reaching.'

pronunciation.approximation: 'tah-ah-ROH-ah' — keep all four vowels pure, tap the r lightly, and let the middle syllable catch on a gentle glottal stop.

kin.label: Tongan–Samoan
kin.form: Tangaloa, the supreme creator of the western Polynesian traditions (Craig, Dictionary of Polynesian Mythology)

kin.label: Māori
kin.form: Tangaroa, god of the sea, son of Ranginui and Papatūānuku (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

kin.label: Hawaiian
kin.form: Kanaloa, god of the deep ocean and of the underworld (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology)

pronunciation.note: Ta'aroa is the Tahitian form of Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa, the name carried across the triangle as Tangaloa, Tangaroa, and Kanaloa. The catalog restoration keeps the older missionary-era spelling used by Henry and Ellis, in which the Tahitian glottal stop is unwritten — a sound DNS cannot carry. Tier 2: no vowel length marks the name; the loss is a display fact, not a judgment of rank.

domains.title: Taaroa
domains.subtitle: Creator
domains.lead: In the old religion of Tahiti, Taaroa is not one god among many but the ground of all divinity — the self-existent one who dwelt alone in the primal darkness, burst the shell of his own being to make sky and earth, and fathered or simply is every other god. The first missionary scholars recorded his cosmogony with respect verging on awe.

cards.name: The Unbegotten
cards.desc: Ta'aroa has no father and no mother: the accounts insist he was never made, because before him there was nothing that could make him.

cards.name: Maker of Sky and Earth
cards.desc: He broke his world-shell: the upper half became the sky, the lower half the earth, and the space between them the living world.

cards.name: Father of the Gods
cards.desc: In the fuller tellings he fashioned the other great gods — Tane, Rono, Tū, 'Oro — and set each over a domain of the world.

cards.name: The Distant One
cards.desc: When creation was finished he withdrew to the highest heaven; every prayer began and ended with his name.

symbols.name: The world-shell
symbols.meaning: The egg-like shell in which Ta'aroa crouched alone in the darkness; when he broke it, sky rose from the upper half and earth spread from the lower (Henry, Ancient Tahiti).

symbols.name: The spiral
symbols.meaning: The ʻōro spiral of growth by which creation proceeds outward from a point — the geometry the priests saw in the unfolding world and in the sacred hair of the gods.

symbols.name: The primal darkness (Te Pō)
symbols.meaning: The night in which Ta'aroa existed alone before anything else; creation is not the defeat of darkness but its self-opening.

symbols.name: The opening invocation
symbols.meaning: Every Tahitian prayer and chant began with Ta'aroa's name and closed with it — the priests named him 'the god of gods' before any other name was spoken (Henry, Ancient Tahiti).

symbols.name: The raised stones of the marae
symbols.meaning: The open-air temple platforms of Tahiti with their carved god-houses (ʻōroʻō); his cult was administered by the highest priesthood of the islands.

mythology.lead: Taaroa's mythology is a cosmogony in the strict sense — an account of how anything at all came to be. The Tahitian priests told it to the first missionaries, and it survives in two nineteenth-century witnesses: the narrative taken down by the missionary John Davies and the longer version preserved by Teuira Henry from the scholars of Papeari.

myths.title: Before There Was Anything
myths.text: The old scholars of Tahiti told the missionary John Davies — and Teuira Henry heard it again two generations later — that before there was sky, sea, land, light, or any other being, Taaroa was. He had no father and no mother, for nothing existed before him that could beget him; his cult name Ta'aroa-'onohi-'ote-na'i-'atu means 'Ta'aroa, the self-existing, the origin of all things.' He dwelt in the primal darkness called Te Pō, wrapped in his own shell like a chick in the egg, calling into the void — and no one answered, because there was no one else to answer. The whole of the world-to-come lay folded inside him, as the tree lies folded in its seed, and the first act of the cosmos was that loneliness outgrew its shell. (Davies' account, preserved in Ellis, Polynesian Researches I; Henry, Ancient Tahiti 336–338.) The myth makes the first moment of existence a soliloquy: creation begins as a being who has no one else to speak to, speaking himself into company.

myths.title: Sky from the Upper Half, Earth from the Lower
myths.text: Weary of confinement, Ta'aroa broke his shell open. The upper half of it he raised high above him and made the sky; the lower half he spread out beneath him and made the earth. From himself he brought forth the sea, the springs, the rocks and sands, the trees and plants, the fish and birds, and the land animals — the whole inventory of the world drawn, item by item, out of his own being, nothing borrowed and nothing left over. In Henry's version he then turned to its government, which is where the third myth begins. (Henry, Ancient Tahiti 336–349; Ellis, Polynesian Researches I.) The image is precise and strange: the cosmos is not built from outside materials but hatched — the world as the broken shell of a god who could no longer bear to be alone.

myths.title: The Maker of Gods and of Men
myths.text: In the fuller tellings, Ta'aroa did not keep the world to himself. He fashioned the other great gods — Tane of the forests and birds, Rono of peace and cultivated food, Tū of war and of humankind, Ta'ata, and the young warrior god 'Oro who would inherit the great national marae — and set each over his portion of creation. He then made men and women to people the earth he had spread. The sources are early and do not always agree on the details — Davies' version, gathered in 1818, is sober where Henry's, drawn from priestly families of Papeari, is expansive — but all agree on the order: gods first, then people, and Ta'aroa before and above both. (Davies in Ellis, Polynesian Researches I; Henry, Ancient Tahiti.) The theology is remarkably austere: a single unbegotten power delegates everything, and rules by having made the rulers.

myths.title: The Distant One Ascends
myths.text: When the work of creation was complete, Ta'aroa did not remain to govern the world day by day. He withdrew to the highest heaven, above the dwelling of Tane and all the other gods, and from that remove he was invoked as 'the god of gods.' Every prayer and every sacrifice on the marae began with his name and ended with his name, whatever lesser deity was being petitioned in between; the priests addressed him as the root from which the other divinities grew, the trunk of which they were branches. It is this withdrawal that his name's traditional gloss — 'the distant one' — is usually taken to mean. (Henry, Ancient Tahiti.) The pattern is the deus otiosus, the resting god familiar from many traditions: having made the world, the creator leaves it running and becomes a direction — the vertical axis toward which all prayer climbs.

lore.syncretism: When the London Missionary Society reached Tahiti in 1797, the first catechists did not find a clutter of squabbling idols — they found a supreme god whose creation narrative sounded uncomfortably like Genesis, and they said so in their journals. Tahitian scholars who worked with them, the deacons of the mission schools, readily compared Ta'aroa to Jehovah, a comparison that eased conversion and ultimately doomed the cult: the great marae were abandoned within a generation, the god-houses burned or left to rot. Ta'aroa survived in the cult of his son 'Oro, whose war-god religion absorbed the national priesthood. In the western islands his own name lived on as Tangaloa, creator of Tonga and Samoa; in Aotearoa it had already become Tangaroa, lord of the sea; in Hawai'i, Kanaloa, god of the deep. One god, three more names, many biographies — the comparative method's favorite case.
lore.culturalLegacy: Taaroa's direct cult ended in the early nineteenth century, but his name never left Tahiti. It lives in the great marae the Polynesian nations are rebuilding: Taputapuātea on Ra'iatea, dedicated to his son 'Oro, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2017 and re-consecrated by delegations from across the triangle. The cosmogony recorded by Henry remains a foundational text of Polynesian studies, taught wherever the old religion is taken seriously as theology rather than curiosity. Contemporary Tahitian dancers and orators invoke Ta'aroa as the name of origins in the renaissance of ʻōrero and ori Tahiti. And because the creation chant opens every traditional ceremony with his name, 'Ta'aroa' has become the shorthand Polynesians reach for when they want to say: this is where we begin.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Most creation stories start with a problem: chaos to be fought, a dragon to be split, a rival to be overthrown. Taaroa's story starts with something rarer — sufficiency. Before there was anything, there was a being who needed nothing: no parents, no materials, no opponent. The world is not a conquest but an overflow, the cracking of a shell that had become too small for the being inside it. And there is a loneliness in this that the myth does not hide: the first thing the god does in the darkness is call out, and no one answers. Creation, on this reading, is not an act of power but of company — the universe as the solution to solitude.

When the work is done, Ta'aroa withdraws to the highest heaven and leaves the world to his children. Power that creates and then steps back is the most difficult kind to imagine, and the Tahitians imagined it — a supreme being whose supremacy consists in having delegated everything and in being, still, the direction of every prayer. That is a theology of confidence: the maker does not need to manage, because the making was perfect. The name Ta'aroa, with its gentle glottal catch like a held breath, is the sound of that confidence.

lore.archaeology: No temple of Ta'aroa survives intact — the LMS converts dismantled the marae — but the stone platforms do: hundreds of paved marae with their upright back slabs (unu) and stepped god-houses (ʻōroʻō) dot the Society Islands, most famously the great complex of Taputapuātea at 'Ōpōa, Ra'iatea (UNESCO World Heritage, 2017). The restored valley marae of 'Ārahurahu in Papeari preserves the setting Henry's informants described. Carved tiki figures attest the anthropomorphic image of the gods: the celebrated figure A'a, from Rurutu in the Austral Islands (British Museum), a deity studded with thirty small figures, is widely read as the creator teeming with the gods and people he brought forth.
